There are really three questions involved here. First, why is it a charge and not a tax? The term "export tax" is understood to refer to the regime in existence up until the commencement of this particular regime. Fifty per cent of the proceeds were made directly available to the province, and 50 per cent were to be redirected by the federal government to the province. The shift from tax to charge marks a shift which takes effect in the new regime.
I agree with the hon. member that in substance a tax is now applied for export compensation purposes. There is no
Oil and Petroleum
more sinister intent involved than that. With regard to the provisions of clause 14(2), that really represents an incorporation by reference mutatis mutandis of the provisions of the Excise Tax Act. The hon. gentleman will recognize that the draughtman's shorthand is to prevent him having to repeat, again in extenso, the provisions which are already in the law in the Excise Tax Act. The third is how does the statute impose the tax or the charge on the Crown, whether federal or provincial? This of course is the question we debated at length this afternoon.
With regard to the federal government it is pursuant to section 16 of the Interpretation Act and the declarations involved in clause 3 of this particular bill, where the tax is imposed on the Crown in the right of Canada, and in due course, with regard to parliamentary action, would be imposed on the national petroleum corporation if it were an exporter of oil. With regard to the imposition of the tax on a provincial Crown corporation, that power is provided by clause 3 of the statute and is further to the provisions- to give the actual jurisprudence-of the case, the Attorney General of British Columbia versus the Attorney General of Canada, 1924 Appeal Cases at page 222, in which the Crown in the right of Canada was entitled to charge customs tax in that particular case against a provincial Crown corporation.

I raised this question in order to get the minister to admit that this is an export tax. I have a different opinion than he has about the right, without the consent of the province, to tax property of the province. If it were not to be a tax how could we proceed in the House by way of a ways and means motion insofar as this particular bill is concerned? Unless it were a tax then it cannot in any way come forward as a ways and means motion and be considered in the House in committee of the whole.
So, we recognize here that if clause 3 falls to the ground this means that what the minister has said flows therefrom also falls to the ground, and that the lynch pin for the authority for the imposition of this so-called charge-I prefer to call it a straight tax-depends upon clause 3. It may be that there might be some judicial challenge on that particular point because it seems to me that the whole idea-and I do not wish to repeat the debate of this afternoon-is a denial of the essence of confederation and the ownership of the resources by the province, and that the federal-government by this bill is trying to arrogate to itself powers it never did have, does not have, and never should have. In any event the minister has cleared up the point. He calls it a tax. Therefore it is a tax. That clears up the procedural point I raised in this regard. I do not agree with the minister's concept, but there it is.

Mr. Chairman, during one of the standing committee meetings I expressed my concern about the heavy burden which was being placed on the personnel of the National Energy Board with the administrative responsibilities which had to be added to their ordinary duties this last year and half. At that time the minister stated that they were strengthening the personnel of the board in the hope that they could carry these extra responsibilities. I do not have to point out to the minister that the administration of the bill now being put to the House will continue to add tremendously to the administrative burden of the National

Energy Board, and therefore the difficulties I noticed this last year and half in carrying out the operations of the National Energy Board will be compounded.
This brings me to my major concern. I was a member of the Diefenbaker administration which set up the National Energy Board. We wanted to give Canadians protection in the handling of their energy, protection they had not had before that time.
The first function of the National Energy Board was a judicial one. It was to decide matters which were brought before it pursuant to the National Energy Board statute. I have observed the actions of the board over this last 14 years, and my criticism has been on this question of administration. I think that the time taken in handling routine applications for changes of facilities along a pipeline, for example, has been too long. This has been costly for people applying, costly for the people intervening, and certainly, in the long run, costly to the consumer who has to pay for all this delay. For my part I would like to see a strengthening, a speeding up and streamlining of this judicial function.
Since there are only a few members on this board, the judicial function should take most of their time. In addition to this judicial function they have another extremely important function, and that is to act as a policy suggestion type of institution.
It was recognized back in 1958 and 1959 that Canadians had to look ahead. They had to be informed continually as to the supply situation. These figures should be provided by an independent and capable board. How much natural gas is it proven that we have? What is the best guess of the potential gas supplies to be found? How much proven oil do we have? How much potential can we expect to have, within a time frame, for the safety of the nation?
The failure of the National Energy Board to carry out these advisory functions, which are clearly laid down in the act as their responsibility, is one of the reasons we have been in this situation for the last two years. When the new chairman took over last year I questioned him on behalf of the opposition to see what his position was on this advisory function. He assured the committee that he would do everything he could to restore the operations of the board in the field of advisory function to the government and to the people of Canada.
Knowing something of the heavy load the board has had to bear these last 15 years, knowing a little bit about the tremendous extra administrative responsibilities of the last year and a half, and then to have added to it all these new responsibilities this legislation will entail, I see trouble down the road purely from an administrative standpoint. I think the minister would be well advised to inform his cabinet colleagues that the National Energy Board structure and the divisions of its duties into judicial, advisory and administrative will have to be radically changed. If the minister would give this advice to his colleagues I think they would respond favourably because the board will be the key for several decades to come in the administration and handling of our energy resources.
I would like to give an example of what concerns me. The changes in the movement of oil around the world have been so radical in the last two years that I doubt if there is
April 17, 1975

a single person in a single oil corporation who fully understands the significance of all these changes. Tonight we heard the hon. member for Dauphin ask questions about what is happening to the heavy and medium crudes of Saskatchewan. This is a classic example of how the resources of the country are hurt by not having staff on a board with time to look ahead and to visualize the impact of their decisions on the various types of producers of oil in Canada.
In the rush of quick decisions which were made last year and in light of the under staffed energy board, no one if about to point his finger at the board. But coming from the province of Saskatchewan and representing a constituency where a large percentage of its wealth depends on the health of the companies operating in nearly a score of oil fields, I see the populations of towns of 2,000 reduced by 20 per cent, 30 per cent and 40 per cent because of the exodus of people working in these fields just because the board, at the request of the government in setting a price, did not think through what the disastrous impact would be from setting that price. When they were raising the price up to $6.50 and raising all grades of crude up the same amount, they did not have time to realize that this would destroy more than a score of small but very valuable oil fields in Saskatchewan.
The hon. member for Dauphin is quite right in suspecting that once a low viscosity oil field has been pumped for 15, 18 or 20 years and it goes out of action for two or three years, it is very marginal and dubious economics as to whether that oil field will be brought into production again. If that oil field is kept pumping constantly and the proper recovery measures are taken constantly, it may last another 10, 12, 15 or 18 years, providing a tremendous value in terms of energy to this country.
It is true that production in south eastern Saskatchewan in only measured in terms of 50,000 or 60,000 barrels per day, but 50,000 or 60,000 barrels per day times the number of day in a year times the number of years left in that field, with proper conservation techniques in the pumping and management of that field, amount to hundreds of millions of dollars over the next decade or so.
There is not only the threat that we lose all the jobs of the people who bought or built homes in this area expecting to have 30 years to work looking after these fields, but there is the fact of the stupidity of this country in not thinking ahead on the significance and impact of these increased taxes on the fields. No one on the Energy Board is to blame for this stupidity because there was not the staff to cope with the subject.
I suspect that what is true in southeastern Saskatchewan is also true in other parts of the west, that an understaffed National Energy Board was doing things which were not intentionally harmful but whose effect was disastrous. Now, a year and a half later, the minister is saying "We made a mistake and now we are consulting with the province of Saskatchewan to see if they cannot alter their royalties". In this particular case two guilty parties, two greedy governments, are trying to grab all the economic rent they can from these oil companies, and so great was their greed that the sum total of their tax liability is greater than 100 per cent.
Oil and Petroleum
When I asked the minister if he had seen the figures he said he had, and that every time they produce a barrel of oil it costs them money. The more honest way of saying it is that they are losing money on every barrel they produce. When companies only produce 20 barrels per day per well, if the number of wells they have is multiplied by 20 cents or 30 cents per barrel, it could come to as much as $20,000 or $30,000 per year. They can only carry that kind of loss so long.
I have in my possession letters giving their liability in exact figures. In one particular case the profit on a particular operation is $4,000 and the tax liability is $6,000. The owner of that operation is not going to keep it operating for too long, I should say.
I am making two points, Mr. Chairman. The first is that we have to strengthen the National Energy Board immediately, both in numbers and by restructuring it to handle these decisions more effectively. At the same time we must give it the quality of manpower that is able to understand the impact of its actions. In the theory of the government at Ottawa, a person who is a highly trained administrator in one field should be able to administer in another and could be taken from any department, put into the National Energy Board, and told to "administer". He might be told by the government to raise the price, but I would suspect that many of those administrators would not know the significance of having mediums or heavy crude and so on. This last mistake I referred to was very costly to oil companies in terms of dollars and cents, but it was also costly to the human beings who work and serve in the oil fields.
I am pleading with the minister, under this clause of the bill, to give high priority (a) to increasing the personnel and National Energy Board staff, and (b) to restructing it so that it can separate the judicial function from the administrative function more clearly. Above all I plead with him not to betray the people of Canada in the future by setting aside the advisory function of the National Energy Board. We have paid heavily for that failure in the last ten or 15 years.
I would repeat that when the minister goes looking for new personnel it is going to be hard to find them among civil servants, who usually have a limited knowledge of oil and gas. He will have to consider seeking them within the oil industry, so it will be necessary to set down very clear guidelines on the question of conflict of interest for these people, and to ask them to abandon all ownership of oil and gas.
I have deliberately taken the time of the committee to make this presentation of my feelings in regard to the National Energy Board, Mr. Chairman. I believe it is an excellent institution which has served this country well, but if it is to grow and be staffed in the usual method of institutions and agencies around Ottawa, we are in for some serious trouble. I hope my proposals are acceptable to the minister and that he can put them to his cabinet colleagues with all the energy he can amass in an attempt to give the country a better break than it has had in the last two years.

April 17, 1975
Oil and Petroleum

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a word by way of explanation. The Board now has the responsibility of determining the export volume from month to month and of issuing export licences from month to month, so it already has substantial administrative responsibility. What we do here is impose upon the person who is to make the judgment and issue the licence a further responsibility which goes along with the basic one of collecting the taxes. We are not creating a separate agency in either the Department of National Revenue or my own department for that purpose. We are trying to minimize the number of government agencies dealing with the transaction.
As the hon. member says, I do not think there can be any question that these further responsibilities will impose a need for additional personnel employed by the board. In the past the entire personnel of the board has come from the private sector. The hon. member mentioned the problem of conflict of interest. In trying to balance that, I think it is essential to have people in this field with practical experience in the oil and gas business rather than take them from some other sector of the government.
There is one point on which I take issue with the hon. member, however. He said that in setting the price the government had not been flexible enough. As I pointed out to the hon. member for Dauphin, the government has been flexible in setting the export tax and this is the result of setting variable export prices for the various commodities. With respect to setting the domestic price, by the agreement of March 27 we set the maximum price.
It was the government of Saskatchewan by choosing to go to the full maximum in these particular qualities of oil that, in effect, made that oil non-competitive in the Canadian market. That was the essence of my observation to the hon. member for Dauphin, and the essence of my conversation with the provincial administration. If they would choose to go to the full maximum price, as they chose with lake crude, and arrange the price for sale in Canada with the customers' discount as in the past, it is the belief of my advisers that there could be an increased flow from these particular fields, and some of the hardships he referred to would not have been felt by the industry.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with the greatest respect to the minister, in the government's headlong rush to control the production of oil and petroleum in Canada we have seen something which is retrograde.
The establishment of the National Energy Board was the subject matter of the Borden Royal Commission on Energy and was set up as an independent body to advise the governor in council of certain action that should be taken by the governor in council, such as the approval of applications for export permits and pipelines. It was an independent body of experts. The National Energy Board was also to consider matters of production and the sale of electrical power.
There is also the question of uranium. All forms of energy were to come under the purview of the board,

which was to advise the cabinet about them. By this bill the National Energy Board is to be set up, first of all, as a tax collecting body. It must administer taxes levied on all petroleum products. Is it to do the same with the export of electricity, if the government should decide it will raid that field as well?
By this decision the government will destroy the independence of the National Energy Board. It is to become merely a further instrument at the behest of the minister and the department.
Certainly the collection of taxes, matters involving the excise tax, and all questions of distraint, recovery, and so on, can come under the Minister of National Revenue. This should not be done by the National Energy Board. After all, the Minister of National Revenue is responsible for customs on the one hand and the excise tax on the other. He collects the premiums payable under the Unemployment Insurance Act and the contributions made under the Canada Pension Plan Act. Why should the Minister of National Revenue not collect this tax and be responsible for the administration of its collection?
The minister opposite feels there would be an economy of personnel if it were done by the board. I suggest there will not be; there will be a different philosophy, a different policy governing the way the tax is collected. The Department of National Revenue possesses expertise in these matters.
My colleague from Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain was right when he said that at the heart of this matter there is a potential conflict of interest. In moving around personnel of the National Energy Board I do not see how the chairman, who is responsible for that board and must advise the cabinet about certain administrative matters, can maintain his sense of independence. The board, in essence, should be composed of experts. Somebody there, some member of the board, will become the administrator charged with the responsibilities given to him by this bill.
It seems to me that a potentially grievous wrong is being inflicted on the National Energy Board. Its value is being affected. I go further than my colleague for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain. I say that all of these administrative provisions should be removed; they should not be the responsibility of the National Energy Board. If we are to have a tax of the kind proposed, its collection and the turning of the moneys over to the Receiver General of Canada should be a matter for the Minister of National Revenue. I think we would see a much tidier administration if that were done.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, this clause is giving me concern. It gives to the governor in council under certain conditions very broad powers with regard to what is in effect the remission, either prospectively or retroactively, of charges which are covered by the clauses with which we have been dealing.
I fear giving this power to any government without some safeguards attached to it. I am particularly concerned about giving it to this government whose track record, from the time of Hal Banks up to the time of the dredging companies, has not been too inspiring with regard to its assessments of people and corporations. We must consider that those who might be the beneficiaries may be some of the large corporations involved in transactions for the sale or shipment of petroleum products to the United States.
The governor in council is given the power solely on the indication by the board that it is in the public interest to so do. What is the public interest? Who is the judge as to what is in the public interest? Does someone on the board pick up the telephone and say "Mr. Minister, I think it is in the public interest that you exempt XY corporation from the payment of these charges"? This clause retroactively permits that a charge paid four months previously can be remitted, or the liability released.
There is presently a means of doing this under the Financial Administration Act. According to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules, authority is given to the governor in council on the recommendation of Treasury Board whenever he, that is the governor in council, considers it in the public interest. There is the same language. The governor in council on a recommendation of Treasury Board may, when he considers it in the public interest so to do, remit any tax, fee or penalty. I notice the word tax here. I listened to the interesting discussion of the hon. member for Edmonton West and the minister. In any event, that is covered by one of the subsections in the Financial

April 17, 1975
Oil and Petroleum
Administration Act, the remission clause, which defines tax as including any tax imposed, duty or toll payable to Her Majesty. I think that is wide enough to cover it.
In addition, there is in the remission provision in the Financial Administration Act, with the necessity for remissions to be reported to the House of Commons in the public accounts with statements, names and amounts in respect of anything over a certain amount. This is what alarms me about clause 12. There is nothing which compels the government, unless the minister can advise that the provisions of the Financial Administration Act are applicable, to state that the government is compelled to publish a list of the exemptions with the names and the amounts.
Why is there the word retroactively? Why was that put in? Are there situations now in existence where the government is contemplating exempting people or corporations from charges for which they normally would have been liable last month, the month before, or the month before that? It may be there is something else in the bill of which I am not aware by which this will have to be done. However, as it now stands, the governor in council on the simple advice from the board, which does not have to be expressed in terms of a written certificate and can be done only by a telephone call, can deem it in the public interest that XY corporation, which three months ago was liable for charges in the amount of $100,000 or $150,000, is now exempt from that charge. Any member of this House is bound to be concerned about a bill which grants such extensive power to the government and its representatives when, side by side with that, is authority to provide for these exemptions.
I would like a more detailed explanation if there are people to whom the retroactive aspect is going to be applied. What assurance can we have from the minister, without us moving amendments, that there will be full and complete disclosure? Has the government decided that the provisions of the Financial Administration Act will be applicable, and will it publish in detail all of the facts surrounding any exemptions with the amounts, names and reasons? I believe this is a very reasonable request bearing in mind the rather awesome powers which this gives to the governor in council.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, may I say a word about the amendment. May I preface my remarks by saying something about the exchange that has been taking place between the minister and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain. I never fail to be amused at the way the minister always suggests that if an oil Company is in any difficulty the provincial government ought to reduce the royalties, forgetting that the oil belongs to the people of the province and that they have a substantial claim.
The federal government has moved into the oil field with a very heavy hand in its most recent budget. In the September, 1974, issue of "The Petroleum Industry of Canada" there is a breakdown of a barrel selling for $6.50.
Oil and Petroleum,
They point out that the amount paid in income tax for Alberta oil prior to the budget was 66 cents; under the budget it will be $1.96. For Saskatchewan income tax was 21 cents; it will now be $1.78. That is a very hefty intrusion by the federal government into the cost of a barrel of oil.
I do not think the minister can altogether avoid his responsibility by saying that whenever a particular section of the oil industry is having difficulty the answer is that it should go to the provincial government and ask for a reduction in royalties. As a matter of fact much of the difficulty that we are having now with respect to the oil industry is because in his recent budget the Minister of Finance introduced a provision whereby royalties paid to the provinces were no longer deductible for income tax purposes. The result of that has been that oil companies are now being asked to pay taxes on an expenditure, something that just has not happened in any other area of the economy.
I sometimes get the feeling that the Minister of Finance and Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources are not playing on the same team. One seems to be pulling one way and the other is pulling in the opposite direction. I think the first ministers' conference which took place last week would at least have had a reasonable chance for success had the heavy hand of the Minister of Finance not intruded to the point where the provinces felt they could no longer either trust the federal government or expect from it any degree of fairness and equity. I express the hope that if on re-examination some of the oil companies in Saskatchewan, where they are handling medium and heavy crude oil with a very high sulphur content, can be reclassified, this is something that should be considered.
With respect to the amendment I agree with what was said by the hon. member for Peace River. When I read clause 12 I was exceedingly perturbed. I recognize-and the explanation of the minister has clarified the point for me-that there is a need for flexibility. I know something of the situation in British Columbia where much of our oil goes across the line, is refined, and brought back again. We depend on Vancouver Island for bunker C, for example, which is processed in the State of Washington. It comes through the Trans Mountain Pipe Line, is shipped across to the United States and then is returned to Canada. So I do not quarrel with the need for flexibility. I agree with the minister's explanation that flexibility is required, both with respect to retroactive exemptions and with respect to making rebates in certain instances.
I am not sure that the amendment proposed by the minister is a very satisfactory solution. It will be better than nothing at all, but we have had some unfortunate experiences with respect to rebates, as the minister will recall. I remember it was only a few years ago when a rebate was made to the Ford Motor Company of Canada of $75 million. I think we spent days and days in the House trying to find out why it received this remission, a very substantial sum of money. I recall that none of the other automobile companies received this concession.
Recalling the extent to which the public accounts committee seems to have difficulty in getting data and is always operating on accounts that are 15 to 18 months old, I am somewhat fearful that the amendment that the min-

April 17, 1975
Oil and Petroleum
ister has proposed is going to meet the situation. I should like the minister to let the clause stand until we meet again so as to see whether he can find some more satisfactory way.
A number of things could be done. There might be a provision that all remissions that are made shall be tabled in the House within 15 days of the House meeting or, if the House is meeting, that they be tabled immediately after coming into the possession of the minister, and then referred to the public accounts committee. It seems to me that this would promote more publicity than merely sending these reports, dealing with what could be very large sums of money, to particular individuals or companies. First of all they should be public knowledge, published in the annual report of the National Energy Board, or tabled in the House within 15 days of the sitting of the House and referred to the public accounts committee. In this way not only the members of the public accounts committee but all members of the House would have an opportunity to see how large these sums are, and to whom they have been remitted.
I also think they ought to be categorized, with some explanation of why the rebates have been granted. Without casting any reflection upon the minister, which is the last thing I would want to do, the fact remains that this could become a gigantic boondoggle. I am sure the minister would not condone that, but the fact is we are passing legislation that is not just for this minister but for any minister of any government that may sit on the treasury benches. We should be extremely careful when we give the government power by order in council to pay back millions of dollars, certainly hundreds of thousands of dollars, and to exempt certain companies or persons from the payment of thousands of dollars. Surely there should be every possible safeguard so as to make sure there is no favouritism or any squandering of public funds. I suggest the proposed amendment could be strengthened very considerably.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-NEED FOR ICEBREAKERS IN NORTHWESTERN ATLANTIC-GOVERNMENT POSITION
TRANSPORT-NEED FOR ICEBREAKERS IN NORTHWESTERN ATLANTIC-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appear tonight to follow up on my question of April 15 to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). My concern is as a result of the bill inadequate icebreaker service. Although my main and specific concern is with regard to my particular district of western Newfoundland, the need exists throughout the region.
This is an annual and persistent problem that I bring to the attention of the government every year. Certainly I have brought it to its attention most of the almost seven years I have had the pleasure to be here, but all I receive is the usual answer that the government will do something about the problem sometime in the future. In this case the minister replied that the government will build more icebreakers when it can pay the bill.
I want to make it clear that I have no quarrel with the officials responsible for the development of icebreakers.
April 17, 1975

They can only do what they can with the equipment on hand. I realize what they must experience when fishermen, port authorities, or freight handlers want their needs fulfilled on a priority basis.
At this very moment the lobster fishing season is about to open in district 11 on the west coast of Newfoundland. As a matter of fact, it opens on Sunday. Further along the coast the season opens May 5. Both these districts include an extended area along the whole of the west coast. They provide for many hundreds of fishermen a livelihood, or at least a large portion of their annual income.
I was surprised when the minister facetiously indicated that the government will provide more icebreakers when it can pay the bill. Through his parliamentary secretary I can tell him with the greatest respect that the bills and compensation fishermen and governments have had to pay over the years as a result of losses to lobster gear and other fishing gear due to ice conditions would have much more than paid the bill required to provide a reasonable and adequate icebreaking capability. It is still the old old story of the apathetic approach Canada takes to the fishing industry. I wonder what will happen over the next two or three months as a result of the lack of protective policy for fishermen. Will we have the same battle, when losses are suffered by fishermen, in trying to recover for losses? The season will again have to start late, with the resulting loss of income to fishermen. The same merry-go-round will persist to the frustration and discouragement of Newfoundland fishermen.
This problem focuses attention on the related need for implementation of an income support program. I was surprised to hear the Minister of State for Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) indicate that it will be another couple of months before it can be put into affect. I feel that he forgot to indicate that the introduction of an income support program is dependent upon the completion of the licensing program now in affect. If that is a fact, the minister's optimism, at least to my mind, leaves some doubt.
Returning to the main topic of my question, I appeal to the minister that some meaningful effort lie made to determine icebreaker needs in collaboration with the efforts of the environment department and the fisheries department in a closely co-ordinated plan to provide an adequate icebreaker service which will support a fast deteriorating fishing industry, something which is the result of this lack of support.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cliff Mclsaac (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-NEED FOR ICEBREAKERS IN NORTHWESTERN ATLANTIC-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) makes reference to a reply given by the minister on April 15, and if I understood the hon. member correctly he implied that the minister was expecting fishermen to pay the bill for the icebreakers. He shakes his head in disagreement. I hope he does disagree because, in reading the minister's reply, that certainly is not what he said or meant.
I think the hon. member is well aware of the cost involved in supplying icebreakers and the fact that costs in this particular area, as well as other areas in the last few years, have gone up dramatically. I think that is exactly what the minister was referring to in his remarks.
I am sure the hon. member knows Canada has been and continues to be in the forefront in icebreaking technology
Adjournment Debate
with regard to hull designs, propulsion systems and techniques of this kind. The ministry has at its disposal about 25 icebreakers, and it is intended to begin building two more this year. Study is under way as to the possibility of a third and larger one.
I might also point out to the hon. member-and this may have some eventual possibilities for the Newfoundland coast-that last winter the ministry conducted very successful research into the use of air cushion vehicles to break up ice. They have broken up ice of quite a thickness. That is the kind of research that is new not only to Canada but to the world.
The hon. member asked on April 15, 1975, what actions were being taken with regard to the specific conditions in his area. As of yesterday the department informed me that all the requests for icebreaker support on the west coast of Newfoundland have been answered. There have been no complaints due to lack of support reported to the ministry. The hon. member may have different reports but, if so, our staff has not seen them.
I am advised that ice has been broken by the Louis St. Laurent, the Sir William Alexander and the Labrador in 12 different harbours on Newfoundland's west coast this spring and that, generally speaking, ice conditions are far better this year than they were last year at this time. That may not be of much consolation to the hon. member, but I believe the coastguard is doing and will continue to do everything it can to help shipping and to develop the kind of technology that would put in service more icebreakers, or more air cushion vehicles, or whatever, to accommodate this area.

CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-SUGGESTION STANDING COMMITTEE QUESTION MR. JOHNSON PRIOR TO CONFIRMATION AS VICE-PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on March 24 I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) if he would make a reference which would allow the Standing Committee on Broadcasting to question Mr. A. W. Johnson prior to the confirmation by the government of his appointment as executive vice-president of the CBC. That request was refused. On April 3 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced the appointment of Mr. Johnson to the position, with the very generally accepted understanding that Mr. Johnson will rise to the presidency of that corporation by 1976.
There are three reasons why I want to discuss this question on the adjournment motion tonight. The first has to do with the very serious continuing uncertainty about who determines the mandate and responsibilities of the CBC on a day to day and year by year basis. I realize there is the statute, but there are also various agencies which are expected to have that power and there has been confusion among them. We are all aware in this House of the celebrated conflict between the CBC and the CRTC. The board of directors of the CBC do not know what their mandate is, where it stops and starts. The standing committee of the House of Commons is similarly in the dark. The question of who is to be interpreting the mandate of the CBC and keep it in touch with Canadian requirements needs to be clarified.

April 17, 1975
Adjournment Debate
The second matter is the general question of why important public appointments have to be made in private. The CBC is important to the nation; it can help to unify us or fragment us. Mr. Johnson himself has said, and I paraphrase him, that it is the most important national institution after parliament. Yet the public had no role in determining what action and what set of ideas is going to guide the future of that institution, nor did parliament have any role in the decision. Parliament was explicity excluded from taking any part at all in even questioning the man who would assume the role. I think it is fair for us, as members of parliament, to ask whether the best man was appointed; whether Mr. A. W. Johnson, for all his qualifications-and I recognize them-is the best man to serve that very important institution at this time in Canada.
Since others have spoken and written in other places of his qualities, let me speak about the weaknesses that should have been examined by the standing committee. For one thing his whole experience has been as a professional public servant. He has served in that rather rarified atmosphere in Regina, Saskatchewan, and Ottawa for almost 30 years. By his training and background he is skilled in compromise but not skilled in innovation. There are those who would argue that innovation is needed in the CBC. He has absolutely no broadcasting experience. He has no particular background in other media or in artistic fields which would help a president of that corporation.
One has to pay some heed to the observation of the Canadian journalist, Christina Newman, who in an article in the Globe and Mail wrote that one of the reasons for this appointment;
... has to do with the ways in which he's unselfishly paid his dues to Liberal regimes for the past 10 years.
Christina Newman there was referring not to partisanship in the normal sense, not to partisanship to a party, but very much to partisanship to a narrow view of Canada, a view which happens to be shared by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and others close to the Prime Minister, such as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). It has become well known that the major reason for Mr. Johnson's appointment to this highly sensitive position was that he learned to get along well with people like the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Prime Minister and shares their views about this country.
His appointment is but the most recent in a series of appointments to important public positions of people who happen to share the view of the Prime Minister of Canada, who happened to share the Prime Minister's views on this diverse nation. I, for one, representing a region and being an individual, do not share that point of view. I think there is a danger in loading the top command positions in Canada with people who have a very particular and certainly not universally held view of the nature of the country. Mr. Johnson joins Mr. Michael Pitfield and the ranks of new deputy ministers who were appointed by the Prime Minister on the pretext they are modern, but who in reality were appointed because they share the Prime Minister's particular view of the country. It might even be suggested that this was the mode of choice of those people who were among the most recently appointed to the Supreme Court of Canada.
So here we have a situation where the command positions in a country that is marked by its diversity are held by people whose personal view is strongly centralist and who seem, on their record, to undervalue the diversity which, in my view, must be nurtured if this very diverse country is to survive. This is true of the CBC. All we know of this man who was appointed in privacy is what we read about him. If it is true of the president to be of the CBC, the situation is particularly dangerous with regard to that corporation which can unify this particular, peculiar country only by reflecting its diversity.
These are reservations which I, as a member of parliament committed to the independence, survival and thriving of the CBC, would have preferred to express before the confirmation of the appointment of Mr. Johnson. But we were not given that opportunity. Instead, we were told that it was none of the business of parliament to look into the ideas of the kind of man who is going to guide the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the next seven years. I think that was an unfortunate development and an unfortunate precedent. That was the second of my reasons for wanting to raise this question tonight.
My third reason has to do with parliament itself. If the responsible standing committee of parliament, the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, which passes and approves the estimates of the CBC, cannot even question the man whose personal opinions, stemming from his personal background, are going to guide what he calls the second most important national institution, for the next seven years, what can we do? I think this is a particularly important question to ask now, since so much of the power to affect the decisions of parliament has been accumulated by the treasury benches and taken away from the committees.

Madam Speaker, the views expressed by my hon. friend, the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark), are well known to my minister, to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts and, indeed, to the whole House. On March 27 the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) responded to a letter from the hon. member through which he supported the views expressed by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) on March 11, 1975, in this House during question period.
Further, Madam Speaker, a motion was put to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts to whom the hon. member had been referred by my minister, a motion which would have directed the chairman of that committee to request the government to make a reference which would have allowed the committee to question the government nominee for the position of executive vice-president of the CBC prior to the confirmation by the government of this nominee. The proposed amendment, Madam Speaker, was negatived.
